v.q: What are the three parts of a JWT?
v.w: The parts are Base64URL encoded and joined by dots. The header names the algorithm and the payload holds the claims.

v.q: Which part of a JWT carries the claims such as sub and exp?
v.w: The header names the algorithm, the payload holds the claims and the signature protects both.

v.q: Is the payload of a normal signed JWT (JWS) secret?
o: No, it is only encoded, so anyone with the token can read it
Yes, it is encrypted with the signing key
Yes, but only while sent over HTTPS
No, because it is always empty by design
v.w: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Never put secrets or sensitive personal data in claims, or use JWE for encryption.

v.q: Which statement about a signed JWT is NOT true?
o: Anyone holding the token can read the claims
A signature does not hide data
v.w: A JWS is signed, not encrypted. Do not put secrets in it. JWE is the encrypted form.

v.q: What does the signature let a resource server verify?
o: That a trusted party issued it and nobody has altered it
That the user is still logged in right now
That the user's password is still correct
That the token has never been used before
v.w: The server verifies the signature with a shared secret (HS256) or the issuer's public key (RS256, ES256). It does not know if the token was revoked.

v.q: Which statement about the JWT signature is NOT true?
o: It proves the user is still logged in
It proves the token was not altered
It proves a trusted key signed it
It does not say whether the token was revoked
v.w: A signature says nothing about the current session. Expiry and revocation checks are separate.

v.q: Which claims should a resource server always validate?
o: Only the user name inside the token
Only the total length of the token
v.w: An expired, wrongly-issued or wrongly-targeted token must be rejected even if the signature is valid. Pin the accepted algorithms too.

v.q: Which check is NOT part of validating an incoming JWT?
v.w: Validate signature, exp, iss and aud and accept only the algorithms you expect.

v.q: A JWT header says `"alg": "none"`. How should a secure server react?
o: Reject it, since only the expected algorithms are accepted
Accept it, because no signature means no risk
Accept it when the caller is an internal user
Switch to HS256 automatically and carry on
v.w: The `alg=none` and RS256-to-HS256 confusion attacks come from trusting the algorithm named in the token. Configure it on the server.

v.q: Which attack makes a server accept a forged token by switching the algorithm?
v.w: Pin the allowed algorithms on the server. Never let the token choose.

v.q: Where is the safest place for a browser app to keep a long-lived refresh token?
v.w: Script-readable storage can be stolen by XSS. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, though you must then defend against CSRF.

v.q: Which storage place is NOT safe for a long-lived refresh token in a browser app?
v.w: Scripts can read localStorage, so one XSS flaw leaks the token.

v.q: Why are access tokens kept short-lived (minutes) and paired with a refresh token?
o: A stolen access token expires fast, and refresh tokens can be revoked
Short tokens are cheaper for the server to sign than long ones
Browsers automatically delete any token that lives too long
Refresh tokens are never kept anywhere on a server
v.w: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked easily. A short lifetime limits exposure and the refresh flow gives the server a revocation point.

v.q: Which statement about refresh tokens is NOT true?
o: They get a new access token
v.w: Long-lived tokens are the risky part, so rotate them and keep them revocable.

v.q: When might you prefer an opaque session id over a JWT?
o: You need instant revocation and server-side control of sessions
You want the system to keep no server state of any kind
Every client must be able to read the claims itself
The credential has to be larger than a normal token
v.w: JWTs are great for stateless APIs between services. Server sessions revoke instantly, but need shared storage when scaled out.

v.q: Which requirement favours an opaque session id over a JWT?
v.w: A server-side session can be deleted at once. A JWT stays valid until it expires.
